pdb2gmx.title: gmx pdb2gmx builds the topology for the simulation
pdb2gmx.intro: p2b2gmx is the first step in setting up a GROMACS simulation. A PDB file only gives the position of each atom, and most crystal structures leave out the hydrogens. pdb2gmx adds the hydrogens the force field expects, decides the charge of every residue, and writes the topology. The topology is the parts list for the simulation, with the type, charge and mass of every atom and every bond between them. At the end of the file it tells you how many sets of molecules are in the system (right now that is just the protein).
pdb2gmx.asks: When you run it, pdb2gmx stops and asks which force field you want to use. Type the number at the prompt in the terminal and press Enter, which will finish the command.
pdb2gmx.stepRef: p2b2gmx flags: -f denotes the input file (lysozyme.pdb here), -o the coordinate file pdb2gmx makes (lysozyme.gro) and -p the topology (lysozyme.top), which gets updated with water and ions in later steps. pdb2gmx also writes posre.itp, which lets us restrain the protein later. The next step is in a GROMACS workflow is editconf.
pdb2gmx.ff.label: force field
pdb2gmx.ff.byName: name it with -ff instead of answering the question
pdb2gmx.ff.note: Picking one here types its number at the prompt for you. 3, which is AMBER19SB is a good, modern forcefield to try first. OPLS-AA/L (number 17) is also a good choice. Some forcefields are protein-only and others include different biomolecules (RNA, carbohydrates, etc.).
pdb2gmx.water.note: -water sets the water model the topology will point to. The waters themselves are added later by solvate. Leave it out and pdb2gmx asks a second question. tip3p is a good general water model for protein simulation, although doesn't polarize like real water (which isn't generally needed).
pdb2gmx.ignh.note: -ignh means ignore the hydrogens in the input .pdb. pdb2gmx then adds its own, with names the force field knows.
pdb2gmx.topLabel: The topology pdb2gmx wrote from the command above:
pdb2gmx.noFile: This folder has {files}. Check the spelling of the file name after -f.
pdb2gmx.badFF: Force field names are the folder names without .ff: {names}.
pdb2gmx.waitFF: pdb2gmx is waiting for you to pick a force field. Type a number from the list and press Enter. In this workflow we answer 1 (AMBER03).
pdb2gmx.waitAgain: pdb2gmx only takes a number from the list. Anything else and it keeps waiting, so type a number from 1 to {n}.
pdb2gmx.waitWater: Without -water, pdb2gmx will ask what water model you use before proceeding. Type the number of the water model. For AMBER03, TIP3P is number 1.
pdb2gmx.waitAgainWater: Type a number from 1 to {n}. pdb2gmx keeps waiting until it gets one unless you enter -ff and the model name in the pdb2gmx command.
pdb2gmx.answered1: You answered 1, so this is AMBER03, the force field we use in this workflow.
pdb2gmx.answeredOther: You answered {n}, so this is {ff}. In this workflow we answer 1 (AMBER03).
pdb2gmx.namedFF: -ff {ff} answers the force field question on the command line, so pdb2gmx doesn't ask. This is handy in a batch job, where nobody is there to type a number.
pdb2gmx.noIgnh: This PDB file has no hydrogens, so leaving out -ignh changes nothing in this run. Structures from NMR or modelling programs often do have hydrogens, usually with names the force field doesn't know, and these incorrect hydrogen names will cause pdb2gmx to stop with an error unless you add -ignh.
pdb2gmx.waterNotListed: {water} isn't in the water list for {ff}. pdb2gmx writes the topology anyway, but the force field was not built with that water.
pdb2gmx.extraQuestions: -{flag} makes pdb2gmx ask extra questions, one for each residue it affects. This page doesn't have those runs, so it shows the result with the default answers.
pdb2gmx.rows.atomsAfter: Atoms in the system after pdb2gmx
pdb2gmx.rows.unitedAtom: united atom, so only polar hydrogens
pdb2gmx.rows.chargeNote: genion will neutralize the system charge
pdb2gmx.rows.waitingNote: Answer the question in the terminal to see what pdb2gmx makes.
genion.title: gmx genion adds ions to the solvated system
genion.intro: genion adds charges to the system by randomly replacing water molecules with ions. It works out how many ions from -conc and the volume of the box, and -neutral adds extra counter-ions so the whole box ends up with zero net charge. Each ion takes the place of one water molecule.
genion.asks: When you run genion, the program lists the groups of atoms in the system and asks which one it may replace with ions. We want it to replace waters, so the answer is SOL (or its number). Type it at the prompt in the terminal and press Enter.
genion.stepRef: Flags for genion: -s tells genion which .tpr file the ions will be added to (the one made by grompp in step 6), -o is the output structure, and -p updates the topology with the ions. It is very important to answer the group question with SOL.
genion.conc.note: Salt concentration in mol/L. We use 0.1 M here as a reasonable approximation as ~0.15 M is the intracellular average for mammalian cells.
genion.neutral.note: Adds extra counter-ions so the total charge of the box is zero.
genion.p.note: Swaps the right number of SOL for NA and CL in the topology. Without it, the next grompp won't match.
genion.names.note: -pname sets the cation (sodium) and -nname the anion (chloride). The names must match a molecule in the force field's ions.itp, and the AMBER and CHARMM force fields in GROMACS use NA and CL.
genion.rmin.note: The closest an ion may be placed to another ion. We use 0.3 nm here, and the default is 0.6 nm.
genion.wrongTpr: genion reads the .tpr made by grompp in step 6, {tpr}.
genion.groNotTpr: It needs a .tpr, not a .gro, because it uses the topology inside the .tpr to know which atoms are water.
genion.noTpr: genion reads the .tpr that grompp made in step 6.
genion.wrongTop: The topology for this system is {top}.
genion.np: -np and -nn set the number of ions directly. This page has runs for -conc with and without -neutral, so take out -np and -nn to see them.
genion.noConc: The page has real runs for -conc from 0 to 0.5 in steps of 0.05.
genion.highConc: Above 0.5 M is unusual outside of salt-effect studies.
genion.nothingToAdd: With -conc 0 and no -neutral there is nothing to add, so genion doesn't even ask for a group. The box keeps its net charge.
genion.wait: genion is waiting for you to pick the group of molecules it may replace with ions. Type SOL (or its number) and press Enter.
genion.waitAgain: That isn't a group in the list. Type a number from 0 to {max} or a group name such as SOL. genion keeps asking until it gets one.
genion.groupNotWater: Group {n} ({name}) is not water. genion replaces whole molecules from the group you pick, so the group has to be made of small identical molecules, and the protein is not. Answer SOL (group {sol}).
genion.groupNotInTop: Group {n} ({name}) holds the right atoms, but with -p genion also has to find that name in the [ molecules ] section of the topology to change it, and the topology calls the water SOL. Answer SOL.
genion.otherWaterGroup: Without -p, genion doesn't touch the topology, so {name} works the same as SOL here.
genion.noP: Without -p the topology still says SOL {nsol} and has no ions, so the next grompp finds {missing} fewer atoms than the topology lists and stops.
genion.netCharge: The box still has a net charge of {net}. With PME, grompp warns about this, and the grompp in step 8 has no -maxwarn, so it would stop there. Add -neutral.
genion.ionNames: genion writes whatever names you give it, but grompp will look for a molecule called {p} or {n} in ions.itp and stop with "No such moleculetype" if it isn't there.
genion.rmin: -rmin is the closest an ion may be placed to another ion. We use 0.3 nm here, and the default is 0.6 nm.
genion.noRmin: Without -rmin, genion keeps ions at least 0.6 nm apart (the default). We lower it to 0.3 nm here.
genion.rows.ofWaters: of {n}, and each ion replaces one
genion.rows.netAfter: Net system charge after adding ions
genion.rows.waitingNote: Answer the group question in the terminal to see where the ions go.
trjconv.title: gmx trjconv cleans up the trajectory
trjconv.intro: mdrun saves every atom where the integrator left it, inside the periodic box. A molecule that drifts through one wall of the box comes back in through the opposite wall, so in the raw trajectory it can look broken or stretched out. This is OK, and trjconv takes care of it. trjconv makes molecules whole, keeps them from jumping across the walls, centers them or fits them onto the first frame, picks which atoms to keep, and thins out the frames so the file is smaller.
trjconv.asks: When you run it, trjconv asks you to pick a group of atoms for each job it does: one for -fit, one for -center, and one for the output. Type the group number (or name) at each prompt in the terminal and press Enter.
trjconv.stepRef: The workflow runs trjconv five times. The first writes a PDB of the minimized system so we can check it in PyMOL or VMD. The other four run on the production trajectory and make smaller files for viewing in VMD.
trjconv.pbc.note: -pbc mol puts each molecule back together, and -pbc nojump follows every atom so the protein and its ions don't jump around with the periodic boundaries.
trjconv.center.note: -center moves the group you pick to the middle of the box. trjconv asks for that group before the output group.
trjconv.fit.note: -fit rot+trans keeps the protein from moving around by superimposing every frame on the first one. Without it, VMD shows the real tumbling, which is hard to watch. trjconv asks which group to fit on (we answer 4, Backbone).
trjconv.dt.note: -dt 10 says to keep one frame every 10 ps. The production run saved a frame every 5 ps.
trjconv.dump.note: -dump 0 tells trjconv to write whatever is going on at time 0 as a single structure instead of a trajectory. VMD uses this as the starting frame.
trjconv.badExt: The extension of -o sets the file type. Use .xtc for a trajectory and .gro or .pdb for a single structure.
trjconv.noInput: trjconv reads the trajectory mdrun wrote, like magainin2_longmd.xtc, or a structure like lysozyme_em_sol.gro.
trjconv.noMDTerm: (no MD run saved for this system yet)
trjconv.noMD: The production run was saved for {systems} only.
trjconv.noS: Give trjconv the run input file with -s. trjconv uses it to know which atoms make up a molecule (for -pbc), which groups you can pick from, and the reference structure for -fit.
trjconv.wrongS: Use the .tpr that made the trajectory, {tpr}.
trjconv.noFrames: No frames are left between -b and -e. The production run covers 0 to 500 ps.
trjconv.wait.fit: trjconv is asking which group to fit on (question {i} of {n}). We answer 4 (Backbone). Type a group number or name and press Enter.
trjconv.wait.centering: trjconv is asking which group to center in the box (question {i} of {n}). We answer 4 (Backbone).
trjconv.wait.output: trjconv is asking which group to write to the output file (question {i} of {n}). We answer 0 (System, every atom). Answer 1 to write only the protein when we don't need the water.
trjconv.waitAgain: That isn't a group in the list. Type a number from 0 to {max} or a group name such as Protein.
trjconv.fitOther: The page shows -fit rot+trans. {fit} removes less of the motion.
trjconv.fitRaw: This fits the raw trajectory, so any frame where the peptide is split across the box gets fitted in pieces. The workflow fits the nojump trajectory from step 17 instead, and that is what is shown here.
trjconv.noPbc: The page has real runs for -pbc none, mol and nojump.
trjconv.pbc.res: -pbc res is like mol, but per residue.
trjconv.pbc.whole: -pbc whole is like mol, without putting molecules back in the box.
trjconv.pbc.cluster: -pbc cluster keeps clusters of molecules together.
trjconv.centerNoPbc: -center without -pbc mol moves the center into the middle of the box but leaves broken molecules broken. Use the two together.
trjconv.nojumpNoCenter: The picture shows the workflow's version, which also has -center. Without it the peptide starts where it was in the box and wanders off from there.
trjconv.waterInOutput: Group {n} ({name}) includes {water} water atoms. They are written to the file but hidden in the picture.
trjconv.systemBig: That makes the file about 100 times bigger than the protein alone.
trjconv.groTrajectory: {n} frames in a .gro file is {size} of text. Use .xtc for trajectories, and .gro or .pdb for single frames (-dump).
trjconv.fitNoBox: After fitting, the box rotates with every frame, so it isn't drawn.
trjconv.pdbCheck: The PDB keeps everything in group {n} ({name}). Open it in PyMOL or VMD to check the minimized system. The protein should be whole and surrounded by water and ions.
trjconv.rows.waitingNote: Answer the group questions in the terminal to see what trjconv writes.
editconf.title: gmx editconf puts the protein in a box
editconf.intro: editconf lets us edit the configuration of the system. Here we use it to put the protein inside a box. The box repeats forever in every direction, so the protein always has copies of itself next door. Change the command or the controls and watch the box, its volume and the gap to the neighbouring copies change.
editconf.asks: editconf won't ask you any questions, it will read the .gro file you give it then print what it did.
editconf.stepRef: Flags for editconf: -f denotes the .gro input file from pdb2gmx (lysozyme.gro). -bt octahedron denotes the box type to put around the protein. -d 2 says to put the box wall at least 2 nm from any protein atom. -o is the output .gro file (lysozyme_b4soln.gro), which is minimized next with grompp and mdrun.
editconf.legend.cell: unit cell written to the .gro file
editconf.d.note: The smallest gap, in nm, between the protein and the box wall. GROMACS sizes the box from the protein's diameter plus twice this number. Going from 2 to 5 makes the system much bigger and the simulation run much slower due to excess water molecules to simulate.
editconf.bt.note: Leave -bt out and you get triclinic, a rectangular box fitted to each axis separately.
editconf.box.note: Sets the box length directly instead of sizing it from the protein.
editconf.c.note: Moves the center of the protein to the center of the box. -d and -box turn this on for you unless you write -noc.
editconf.groLine: Last line of {file}. These numbers set the box shape and size in nm.
editconf.footer: The numbers on this page are computed the same way GROMACS does it and were checked against real gmx editconf runs. Water counts are estimates fitted to real gmx solvate runs on these two structures. Lysozyme coordinates come from PDB 2LYZ.
editconf.noFile: This folder has {files}, made by pdb2gmx. See how they were made.
editconf.vsCube: {n}% smaller than a cube with the same -d
editconf.gap.label: Closest approach to a periodic copy
editconf.gap.bad: This is less than the {cut} nm cutoff, so the protein would interact with its own copy in an adjacent box. Make the box bigger.
editconf.gap.warn: This clears the {cut} nm cutoff for now, but there is little room to spare if the protein turns or changes shape.
editconf.gap.ok: This is more than twice the {cut} nm cutoff, so the protein can tumble without meeting its own copy.
editconf.noSize: There is no -d or -box, so editconf keeps the box from the input file. pdb2gmx wrote one that just fits the protein ({size} nm). Add -d 1.0 to size the box around the protein.
editconf.dWins: With a triclinic box, -d wins and -box is ignored.
editconf.boxWins: With this box type, -box wins and -d is ignored. Use one or the other.
editconf.oneLength: A {bt} box has one length, so GROMACS uses only the first -box value.
editconf.notCentered: The protein is not centered, so it keeps its coordinates from the input file and can hang outside the box. The box repeats, so the physics is fine, but the system is hard to check by eye. Leave out -noc.
editconf.negD: A negative -d makes the box smaller than the protein.
editconf.triclinic: GROMACS warns because each side was fitted separately. A long molecule that turns can end up close to its own copy. Try -bt cubic or -bt dodecahedron.
editconf.notDrawn: {flag} is a real editconf option, but this page doesn't draw it yet.
editconf.groOut: Give -o a .gro name so the next step can read it.
system.lysozyme.name: Hen egg-white lysozyme
system.lysozyme.source: PDB 2LYZ heavy atoms (the same protein as 1AKI in the Lemkul tutorial). 129 residues, net charge +8, with 4 disulfide bonds.
system.magainin2.name: Magainin 2 (antimicrobial peptide)
system.magainin2.shape: A single long helix, about 3.8 nm end to end.
system.magainin2.source: GIGKFLHSAKKFGKAFVGEIMNS from frog skin, built as an ideal α-helix. 23 residues, net charge +3.
solvate.title: gmx solvate adds water
solvate.intro: solvate tells GROMACS how water will be added to the system. It copies a small box of pre-relaxed water over and over until the box is full, then deletes every water that overlaps the protein or another water. With -p it also adds the new waters to the topology. The waters added to the system are generally in an ordered array, so an energy minimization is usually run to make the water structure more normal (i.e. random) before running production simulations.
solvate.asks: solvate doesn't ask you any questions. It reads the files you give it, fills the box with water molecules and prints how many waters it added.
solvate.stepRef: Flags for solvate: -cp tells solvate which system we are solvating, which in this case is the protein minimized in vacuum in step 4. -cs spc216.gro is a pre-relaxed box of 216 waters, so we don't have to add each water by hand. -o is the outputted solvated system (lysozyme_b4ion.gro) that genion uses in the next phase. -p updates the topology file with the waters we just added. We can't solvate the same system twice, so if something goes wrong start again from pdb2gmx. Fortunately all commands except mdrun only take a few seconds to run, so rebuilding is quick.
solvate.view.slice: Slice through the middle of the box
solvate.cs.note: spc216.gro holds 216 relaxed 3-site waters. It works for SPC, SPC/E and TIP3P, because the topology decides the water model.
solvate.p.note: Adds a SOL line to the topology so it knows about the new waters.
solvate.oneAtATime: Each of these settings was run on its own, so change one at a time.
solvate.laterStep: {file} is made by a later step ({step}).
solvate.soluteFiles: The solute files at this step are {files}.
solvate.badCs: GROMACS looks for -cs in its own library. The water boxes it comes with are spc216.gro, tip4p.gro and tip5p.gro.
solvate.noCombo: This page has real runs that change one thing at a time: -box 7 or -box 10, -maxsol 2000 or 8000, -cs tip4p.gro, or -cp {M}.gro. Pick one from the panel.
solvate.noP: Without -p the topology still lists only the protein, so it describes {top} atoms while the new .gro has {gro}. See what grompp says next.
solvate.pdb2gmxBox: {M}.gro still has the box from the PDB file, which is barely bigger than the protein. Run editconf first.
solvate.tip4p: tip4p.gro waters have 4 sites, but the topology uses 3-site TIP3P. grompp will find more atoms than the topology describes.
solvate.maxsol: The box is only {pct}% full. Pressure coupling would crush it.
solvate.boxFlag: -box replaces the octahedron from editconf with a {n} nm cube, and solvate does not center the protein in it. Set the box in editconf instead, where -c centers it.
solvate.b4soln: We use {M}_em_vac.gro, the minimized protein. {M}_b4soln.gro is the same box before minimization. The water count is almost the same, but the bad contacts in the protein have not been relaxed.
step.pdb2gmx: Adds hydrogens, applies the force field and writes the topology.
step.editconf: Puts the protein in a truncated octahedron box with at least 2 nm between the protein and the box wall.
step.grompp_em_vac: Packages an energy minimization of the protein in vacuum.
step.em_vac: Relaxes bad contacts in the protein before any water is added.
step.solvate: Fills the box with water and adds the waters to the topology.
step.grompp_ion: Packages the solvated system so genion can read it.
step.genion: Swaps waters for Na⁺ and Cl⁻ to neutralize the system and add 0.1 M salt.
step.grompp_em_sol: Packages an energy minimization of the whole solvated system.
step.trjconv_pdb: Writes a PDB copy of the system to check in PyMOL or VMD.
step.em_sol: Minimizes the solvated system so the water fits snugly around the protein.
step.pr: Heats the system to 300 K and settles the water while springs hold the protein in place.
step.grompp_md: Packages a short run without restraints.
step.md: Lets the whole system settle at 300 K and 1 bar.
step.longmd: The production run. This is the trajectory we analyze.
step.trjconv_nojump: Keeps the protein whole and centered for viewing.
step.trjconv_start: Saves the first frame, which VMD uses to load the trajectory.
step.trjconv_fit: Removes the tumbling so we can watch the protein change shape.
step.trjconv_fitstart: Saves the first frame of the fitted trajectory.
grompp.title: gmx grompp packages a run
grompp.intro: grompp (GROMACS preprocessor) takes the parameter file (.mdp), the input structure (.gro) and the topology (.top) and makes a new .tpr file, which is a package file ready to go for simulation. grompp checks that the three inputs agree, so most setup mistakes are caught by grompp.
grompp.asks: grompp doesn't ask you any questions, it will print NOTEs and WARNINGs as it reads the files. A NOTE never stops grompp, but a WARNING will stop it unless -maxwarn with a number (such as -maxwarn 2). Make sure to read the warnings, since they can save you from running a messed up system.
grompp.stepRef: The workflow we're using runs grompp six times, once before each mdrun and once so genion can read the solvated system. -f is the parameter file, -c the input structure made by the previous command, -p the topology, and -o the output package that mdrun runs. Pick a step on the right to see how grompp responds.
grompp.maxwarn.note: How many warnings grompp may ignore. A NOTE never stops grompp, but a WARNING does.
grompp.mdpNote: Highlighted lines are the ones that make this step different from the others. Hover over any line to see what the setting does. Tap or click to keep the label open.
grompp.later: {file} is made by a later step ({step}), so it doesn't exist yet at this point in the workflow.
grompp.notInFolder: There is no {file} in the folder at this step.
grompp.mismatch: The .gro has {gro} atoms and the topology lists {top} ({diff}). {why} Use the coordinates written by the step just before this one.
grompp.earlier: {c} is from before {tool}, but {p} has already been updated by {by}.
grompp.laterCoords: {c} comes from later in the workflow than the topology at this step.
grompp.posres: define = -DPOSRES in the .mdp turns on the springs from posre.itp. Add -r with the structure the springs should hold the atoms to. We use the same file as -c.
grompp.maxwarn: PME electrostatics with a net charge of +{q} gives one WARNING, and the default -maxwarn is 0.
grompp.maxwarnIon: At this step the warning is expected. This .tpr is only read by genion, which removes the charge. That is why we add -maxwarn 1 here.
grompp.maxwarnOther: Use em_vac.mdp (cut-off Coulomb) before the ions are added, or add the ions first.
grompp.noSaved: (The runs used for this exercise did not save this exact combination. grompp accepts it and writes the .tpr. Read the notes below.)
grompp.letThrough: -maxwarn {n} let the net charge warning through.
grompp.letThroughIon: This is fine for the genion step, because this .tpr is only read and never run.
grompp.letThroughOther: This .tpr would run a charged system with PME. Neutralize it with genion instead.
grompp.moreThanNeeded: -maxwarn {n} is more than needed. It is harmless now, but it would hide a new warning if something changes later.
grompp.notNeeded: -maxwarn {n} is not needed here because there are no warnings. It is harmless now, but it would hide a new warning if something changes later.
grompp.rIgnored: -r is only read when the .mdp turns on restraints (define = -DPOSRES). {mdp}.mdp doesn't, so it is ignored.
grompp.vacWithWater: em_vac.mdp uses a plain cut-off for Coulomb. That is fine in vacuum, but with water around the protein it gives poor electrostatics. Use em_sol.mdp (PME) once the box is solvated.
grompp.noVelocities: {mdp}.mdp has continuation = yes and gen_vel = no, so it expects velocities from the previous MD run. {c} has none, so every atom would start at rest.
grompp.scriptUses: This step of the workflow uses {mdp}.mdp.
grompp.card.rUsed: pr.mdp holds heavy atoms near these positions
grompp.card.rUnused: only read when the .mdp has define = -DPOSRES
grompp.card.err.posres: The restraints have no reference positions.
grompp.card.package: Everything mdrun needs in one file: the parameters, {n} atoms with their starting positions, and the force field.
grompp.state2: protein, water and ions (genion swapped some SOL for NA and CL)
grompp.topNote: At this step the topology holds the {state}. Its last section must list the molecules in the same order and number as the .gro.
mdrun.title: gmx mdrun runs the simulation
mdrun.intro: mdrun is the program that runs simulations. It reads the .tpr package from grompp and either minimizes the energy or moves the atoms forward in time. Everything about what is simulated is already in the .tpr. The options we give mdrun only say where the files go and how to use the hardware.
mdrun.asks: mdrun asks no questions. With -v it is loud and noisy, printing its progress until the run is done.
mdrun.stepRef: The workflow we're following runs mdrun five times, including equilibrating the system and running the production simulation. -deffnm sets the default file name for every file mdrun reads and writes. -v gives verbose output during the run. These are real runs, played back frame by frame. Drag the slider or click a chart.
mdrun.deffnm.note: One name for every file. mdrun reads NAME.tpr and writes NAME.gro, .log, .edr and the trajectory.
mdrun.v.note: Verbose output. mdrun prints each minimization step, or the time left in an MD run.
mdrun.noDeffnm: Without -deffnm or -s, mdrun looks for topol.tpr. Add -deffnm with the name you gave the -o of grompp, without .tpr.
mdrun.deffnmExt: -deffnm takes the name without an extension, because mdrun adds .tpr itself. Try -deffnm {name}.
mdrun.noTpr: There is no {tpr}. The .tpr files grompp writes in this workflow are named like {example}.
mdrun.noMDTerm: (no MD run saved for this system yet)
mdrun.noMD: The MD steps were run for {systems} only.
mdrun.nstepsTerm: (the run stops at -nsteps, but the saved run went on to converge)
mdrun.gpuTerm: (GPU lines go here: "1 GPU selected for this run" and how the work is split. This run was made on a CPU-only machine.)
mdrun.defaultNames: Without -deffnm the outputs get default names (confout.gro, md.log, ener.edr, traj.trr). The next mdrun would overwrite them, and the next grompp would not find the file it expects.
mdrun.emSolName: The genion output is named {M}_em_sol.gro, and -deffnm {M}_em_sol writes the minimized structure to the same name. mdrun backs up the old one as #{M}_em_sol.gro.1#. This works, but a different name for the genion output (like {M}_ions.gro) would be clearer.
mdrun.nsteps: -nsteps {n} overrides the .mdp. This is handy for a quick test of the hardware flags, but don't use it for a real run.
mdrun.ranks: With {n} ranks, mdrun splits the box into {n} domains. For a system this size, one rank with many threads is usually faster.
mdrun.cpi: -cpi continues from a checkpoint (.cpt). We use it when a Slurm job hits its time limit. Run the same command again with -cpi NAME.cpt and mdrun picks up where it stopped.
mdrun.hw.splitRanks: the box is split between ranks
mdrun.hw.allCores: auto, all the cores it can see
mdrun.rows.framesNote: every nstxout steps, when the step was accepted
mdrun.rows.target1: target 1 bar, and big swings are normal
mdrun.rows.cpu: on a small CPU-only test machine. Geiss-01 with a GPU is much faster.
mdrun.file.groEM: the minimized structure, which is the input for the next grompp
mdrun.file.groMD: the last frame, with velocities, which is the input for the next grompp
mdrun.file.log: the full log with the settings, hardware, energies and timing
mdrun.file.edr: energies over time, read with gmx energy
mdrun.file.xtc: the compressed trajectory that we analyze and watch
mdrun.file.cpt: a checkpoint, to restart with -cpi if the job is stopped
mdrun.chart.fmaxNote: Minimization stops when this drops below emtol.
mdrun.chart.epotEMNote: Falls fast as bad contacts are relaxed, then levels off. The first few steps are off the top of the chart.
mdrun.chart.tempNote: The thermostat (V-rescale) holds it near 300 K.
mdrun.chart.pressureNote: Swings by hundreds of bar. The average is what counts.
mdrun.chart.densityNote: Settles near 1000 kg/m³ as the box adjusts.
mdrun.chart.epotNote: Flat once the system has equilibrated.
index.title: From a PDB file to a trajectory
index.intro: These are the commands that take a protein from a PDB file to a trajectory, in the order we run them. We type each one at the command line by itself, or they can be run from a shell script (.sh) to automate setup and running simulations. Click a command to open a page where you can change the command and see what it does, using real output from running the commands on two proteins.
index.asks: Some commands stop and ask a question while they run. GROMACS prints the question and waits for your answer. Each of these steps shows the question and the answer we give.
index.pick: Pick a protein to fill in the file names:
index.footer: Runs come from GROMACS with stand-in .mdp files (see workflow/Functions/).
index.noMD: Only the setup and minimization steps were run for this one, so the MD steps link to {other}.
index.loadError: Could not load the example data. Open this page through the local server (node serve.mjs).
index.stage1: Build the topology from the pdb file
index.stage2: Put a box around the protein and relax it in vacuum
index.stage3: Add water and ions to the simulation box
index.stage4: Minimize the solvated system to allow waters to settle
index.stage5: Equilibrate the system to remove steric clashes, overlapping atoms, and unphysical geometries from the model
index.stage7: Make the trajectory easy to watch
ask.pdb2gmx: pdb2gmx lists the force fields it knows and waits. We answer 1, which is AMBER03.
ask.genion: genion lists the groups of atoms in the system and asks which one it may replace with ions. We answer SOL, the water.
ask.trjconv_pdb: trjconv asks which group to write. We answer 0 (System), so the PDB has every atom.
ask.trjconv_nojump: trjconv asks two questions. The first is the group to center, anwering 4 (Backbone) will place the backbone in the center if the trajectory. The second is the group to write, answering 0 (System) will save the entire system. Centering will put the protein in the center, but it can still spin around and be hard to follow. You'll also need to fit the protein to get the protein to stay in one position during the trajectory.
ask.trjconv_start: trjconv asks which group to write. We answer 0 (System).
ask.trjconv_fit: trjconv asks two questions. The first is the group to fit on, answering 4 (Backbone) will fit the trajectory to the protein backbone. The second is the group to write, answering 0 (System) will save the entire system once the trajectory is fit to the protein backbone. Fitting will keep the protein in one position, but it can still be off-center in the trajectory. Most of the time we center the protein so it doesn't move into an adjacent box.
ask.trjconv_fitstart: trjconv asks which group to write. We answer 0 (System).
common.notRun: Press Run or Enter to run this command. What GROMACS prints, and any questions it asks, will appear here.
file.note: These are the real files this step of a GROMACS workflow. Long files are cut down to the parts worth reading. Click a gray bar to show more of the lines in between.
file.notRun: Run the command to see the files it makes.
file.hint: Hover over any part of the file to see what it does. Tap or click to keep the label open.
file.hidden: {n} more lines here. Click to show {m} of them.
file.missing: We don't have a copy of {name} in the visualizer yet.
file.kind.gro: {name} is a coordinate file in GROMACS format. It lists every atom and where it is in nm. Files written by mdrun also have the velocities. The last line is the box.
file.kind.top: {name} is the topology. It tells GROMACS what the molecules are, including every atom with its type and charge, which atoms are bonded and how many of each molecule the system holds. pdb2gmx writes the topology (.top) file, and solvate and genion update the [ molecules ] list at the bottom of the top file.
file.kind.itp: {name} is an include topology file. The .top pulls it in with an #include line. pdb2gmx writes posre.itp with a spring for every heavy atom of the protein, and we use it when the .mdp switches on position restraints.
file.kind.mdp: {name} is the parameter file (molecular dynamics parameters). .mdp files set what kind of run mdrun does, including minimization or dynamics, how long the simulation is, how often to save, and how to handle temperature, pressure and long range forces. grompp reads the .mdp file and packs the settings into the .tpr.
file.kind.tpr: {name} is the run input file. grompp packs the coordinates, the topology and the .mdp settings into this one binary file, so mdrun needs nothing else. It is not a text file, so you can't directly read it. gmx dump -s {name} prints what is inside.
file.kind.edr: {name} is the energy file. mdrun writes the energies, temperature, pressure and density to it as the run goes. It is binary, which you can't read directly. We read it with gmx energy -f {name}, which is how the plots on the mdrun page were made.
file.kind.trr: {name} is a full precision trajectory with coordinates, and velocities and forces when the .mdp asks for them. It is binary and can get large.
file.kind.xtc: {name} is a compressed trajectory that contains the coordinates of every saved frame at reduced precision, which keeps the file small. It is binary that can't be read directly. This is the file you'll read with VMD and PyMOL in addition to a .gro or .pdb file to show the simulation. trjconv is used to manipulate and clean it up for visualization and analysis.
file.kind.cpt: {name} is a checkpoint file. It holds the full state of the run at a particular time, so mdrun can continue with -cpi {name} if the job stops. It is binary that is not human readable.
file.kind.log: {name} is the mdrun log. It records the settings, the hardware mdrun used, the energies every nstlog steps and, at the end, how fast the run was. When a run fails, this is the first place to look for what happened.
file.kind.pdb: {name} is a PDB file, the format most viewers read. trjconv wrote it from the GROMACS coordinates. PDB files use Å, not nm.
file.gro.title: The title line. GROMACS copies it from the input file. Frames written during a run also carry the time in ps (t=).
file.gro.count: The number of atoms in the file ({n}). GROMACS reads exactly this many atom lines, and the line after them is the box.
file.gro.resnr: Residue number (columns 1 to 5). All atoms of one amino acid, one water or one ion share a number. Past 99,999 the number starts again at 0, because the column only has room for five digits.
file.gro.resname: Residue name (columns 6 to 10), such as LYS for lysine, SOL for a water, and NA or CL for an ion.
file.gro.atom: Atom name (columns 11 to 15). N, CA, C and O are the backbone, with CA the alpha carbon. OW, HW1 and HW2 are the atoms of a water.
file.gro.atomnr: Atom number (columns 16 to 20). Atoms are counted from 1 in the order they appear, and that order has to match the topology. Past 99,999 the number starts again at 0.
file.gro.xyz: The x, y and z position of the atom in nm, three decimals each. GROMACS works in nm, so 0.1 nm is 1 Å.
file.gro.vel: The x, y and z velocity in nm/ps. Only files that mdrun writes have these. pdb2gmx, editconf, solvate and genion don't, because nothing is moving yet.
file.gro.box: The box: its length along x, y and z in nm. A rectangular box needs only these three numbers.
file.gro.boxTric: The box vectors in nm. The first three numbers are the lengths along x, y and z. The other six say how the box is slanted, which is how GROMACS stores a triclinic box like our octahedron. editconf set the shape with -bt and the size with -d.
file.top.header: The header pdb2gmx writes: who made the file, when, with which GROMACS and with which command. Lines that start with a semicolon are comments, so GROMACS skips them.
file.top.comment: A comment. GROMACS ignores everything after a semicolon. It is there for us to read.
file.top.residue: A comment pdb2gmx adds at the start of each residue. It gives the residue number and name, the building block (rtp) it used from the force field, and the charge of the residue (q).
file.top.qtot: qtot {q} is the running total of the charge up to this atom. On the last atom of the protein it is the net charge of the whole protein, which genion later cancels with ions.
file.top.colhead: A comment that names the columns of the rows below it.
file.top.include.forcefield: #include pastes another file in at this point, as if its text were typed here. This one brings in the force field ({file}): the atom types, the bond, angle and dihedral parameters, and the rules for nonbonded forces. It has to come before any molecule.
file.top.include.posre: Pulls in {file}, the position restraints pdb2gmx wrote for the protein. It sits inside #ifdef POSRES, so GROMACS only reads it when the .mdp has define = -DPOSRES.
file.top.include.water: Pulls in the water model ({file}) we picked with -water in pdb2gmx. It defines a molecule called SOL, and solvate fills the box with copies of it.
file.top.include.ions: Pulls in the ions of the force field ({file}), such as NA and CL. genion uses these names with -pname and -nname.
file.top.include.other: Pulls in {file} at this point, as if its text were typed here.
file.top.ifdef.POSRES: Everything between this line and #endif is only used when POSRES is defined. We switch it on with define = -DPOSRES in the .mdp (pr.mdp does this). That holds the heavy atoms of the protein in place while the water settles around it.
file.top.ifdef.POSRES_WATER: Only used when POSRES_WATER is defined (define = -DPOSRES_WATER in the .mdp). It would hold every water oxygen in place. We don't use it in this workflow.
file.top.ifdef.other: Everything until #endif is only used when {name} is defined with define = -D{name} in the .mdp.
file.top.else: What follows is used when the #ifdef above is not defined.
file.top.define: Defines {name}, which switches on any #ifdef {name} block below.
file.top.sec.defaults: [ defaults ] sets rules for the whole force field, such as how van der Waals parameters of two atom types are combined and how much 1-4 interactions are scaled down.
file.top.sec.atomtypes: [ atomtypes ] lists every atom type with its mass, charge and van der Waals parameters.
file.top.sec.moleculetype: [ moleculetype ] starts a new molecule. Everything below it, up to the next [ moleculetype ], describes this one molecule. The name is what [ molecules ] uses at the end of the file. nrexcl 3 means atoms up to three bonds apart don't get the normal nonbonded forces between them, because the bond, angle and dihedral terms already describe them.
file.top.sec.atoms: [ atoms ] lists every atom of the molecule: its number, its force field atom type, its residue, its name, its charge and its mass. The order has to match the atoms in the .gro file exactly.
file.top.sec.bonds: [ bonds ] lists every pair of bonded atoms by atom number. The spring constant and the bond length come from the force field, so each row only needs the two atoms and the function type.
file.top.sec.pairs: [ pairs ] lists atoms that are three bonds apart (1-4 pairs). They still feel nonbonded forces, but scaled down as [ defaults ] says.
file.top.sec.angles: [ angles ] lists every set of three bonded atoms. A spring from the force field keeps the angle between them near its ideal value.
file.top.sec.dihedrals: [ dihedrals ] lists sets of four atoms whose twist is controlled. AMBER topologies have two of these sections. The first (function 9) has the proper dihedrals, the rotations around bonds. The second (function 4) has the improper dihedrals, which keep rings and peptide bonds flat.
file.top.sec.cmap: [ cmap ] adds a correction map for the backbone phi and psi angles. CHARMM force fields use it.
file.top.sec.position_restraints: [ position_restraints ] puts a spring on each listed atom that pulls it back toward its starting position. The force constants are in kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> nm<sup>-2</sup>.
file.top.sec.settles: [ settles ] keeps each water molecule rigid. That is faster and lets us use a 2 fs time step.
file.top.sec.exclusions: [ exclusions ] lists pairs of atoms that should not get nonbonded forces between them.
file.top.sec.system: [ system ] gives the system a name. GROMACS copies it into the title of the files it writes. It doesn't change the simulation.
file.top.sec.molecules: [ molecules ] says how many of each molecule are in the system, in the same order as the atoms in the .gro file. pdb2gmx writes the protein line, solvate adds the SOL line, and genion lowers the SOL count and adds the ions. If these counts don't match the .gro file, grompp stops with an error.
file.top.sec.other: [ {name} ] starts a new section of the topology.
file.top.col.atoms.nr: Atom number within this molecule. Bonds, angles and dihedrals refer to atoms by this number.
file.top.col.atoms.type: The force field atom type. It sets the van der Waals parameters and decides which bond, angle and dihedral parameters apply. CT, for example, is a carbon with four single bonds.
file.top.col.atoms.atom: Atom name, the same as in the .gro file.
file.top.col.atoms.cgnr: Charge group number. Older GROMACS versions used it. The Verlet cutoff scheme we use ignores it.
file.top.col.atoms.charge: Partial charge on the atom, in units of the charge of an electron. The charges in one residue add up to a whole number.
file.top.col.atoms.mass: Mass of the atom in g/mol.
file.top.col.atoms.typeb: Atom type in state B. Only free energy calculations use it, so it is empty here.
file.top.col.atoms.chargeb: Charge in state B. Only free energy calculations use it, so it is empty here.
file.top.col.atoms.massb: Mass in state B. Only free energy calculations use it, so it is empty here.
file.top.col.ai: First atom, by its number in [ atoms ].
file.top.col.funct: Function type. It picks the form of the energy term. For bonds and angles, 1 is a harmonic spring. For dihedrals, 9 is a proper dihedral and 4 an improper one.
file.top.col.c0: Parameter column. It is empty here, so GROMACS looks up the parameters in the force field from the atom types. A number here would override the force field.
file.top.col.c1: Parameter column. It is empty here, so GROMACS looks up the parameters in the force field from the atom types. A number here would override the force field.
file.top.col.c2: Parameter column. It is empty here, so GROMACS looks up the parameters in the force field from the atom types. A number here would override the force field.
file.top.col.c3: Parameter column. It is empty here, so GROMACS looks up the parameters in the force field from the atom types. A number here would override the force field.
file.top.col.c4: Parameter column. It is empty here, so GROMACS looks up the parameters in the force field from the atom types. A number here would override the force field.
file.top.col.c5: Parameter column. It is empty here, so GROMACS looks up the parameters in the force field from the atom types. A number here would override the force field.
file.top.col.moleculetype.name: The name of the molecule. [ molecules ] at the end of the file refers to it by this name.
file.top.col.nrexcl: How many bonds apart two atoms must be before they get the normal nonbonded forces. 3 is the usual value.
file.top.col.position_restraints.atom: The atom to restrain, by its number in [ atoms ].
file.top.col.position_restraints.i: The atom to restrain, by its number in its molecule. For water, atom 1 is the oxygen.
file.top.col.position_restraints.type: Function type. 1 is a harmonic spring.
file.top.col.position_restraints.fx: Force constant of the spring along x, in kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> nm<sup>-2</sup>. 1000 holds the atom near its place but still lets it jiggle.
file.top.col.position_restraints.fcx: Force constant of the spring along x, in kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> nm<sup>-2</sup>. 1000 holds the atom near its place but still lets it jiggle.
file.top.col.position_restraints.fy: Force constant of the spring along y, in kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> nm<sup>-2</sup>. 1000 holds the atom near its place but still lets it jiggle.
file.top.col.position_restraints.fcy: Force constant of the spring along y, in kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> nm<sup>-2</sup>. 1000 holds the atom near its place but still lets it jiggle.
file.top.col.position_restraints.fz: Force constant of the spring along z, in kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> nm<sup>-2</sup>. 1000 holds the atom near its place but still lets it jiggle.
file.top.col.position_restraints.fcz: Force constant of the spring along z, in kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> nm<sup>-2</sup>. 1000 holds the atom near its place but still lets it jiggle.
file.top.col.molecules.compound: The name of the molecule. It has to match the name in one of the [ moleculetype ] sections.
file.top.col.molecules.#mols: How many copies of the molecule are in the system.
file.top.col.system.name: The name of the system.
file.top.row.moleculetype: The name of the molecule and its nrexcl. The name is what [ molecules ] uses at the end of the file.
file.top.row.atoms: One atom: its number, atom type, residue number, residue name, atom name, charge group, charge and mass. Hover over the column names above it for more.
file.top.row.bonds: One bond between two atoms, by atom number. Function 1 is a harmonic spring, with its parameters taken from the force field.
file.top.row.pairs: One 1-4 pair: two atoms that are three bonds apart.
file.top.row.angles: One angle between three bonded atoms. The middle atom is the corner of the angle.
file.top.row.dihedrals.9: One proper dihedral: four atoms in a chain, and the twist around the bond in the middle. Function 9 lets the force field add several terms for the same four atoms.
file.top.row.dihedrals.4: One improper dihedral (function 4). It keeps a group flat, such as a ring or a peptide bond.
file.top.row.dihedrals: One dihedral: four atoms and the twist between them.
file.top.row.position_restraints: One restrained atom: its number, the function type (1 is a harmonic spring), and the force constant along x, y and z.
file.top.mol.protein: One protein, called {name} in its [ moleculetype ]. pdb2gmx wrote this line.
file.top.mol.water: {n} waters (SOL). solvate added this line when it filled the box. genion lowers the number when it swaps waters for ions.
file.top.mol.ion: {n} {name} ions, added by genion. They come after the water, in the same order as in the .gro file.
file.mdp.define: define = {value}. Switches on #ifdef blocks in the topology. -DPOSRES turns on the position restraints from posre.itp, which hold the protein in place while the water and ions settle.
file.mdp.integrator: integrator = {value}. steep is steepest descent energy minimization, which moves atoms downhill until the forces are small. md is molecular dynamics with the leap-frog integrator. We minimize first so the first steps of dynamics don't blow up.
file.mdp.dt: dt = {value}. The time step in ps. 0.002 ps is 2 fs, which works because the bonds to hydrogen are constrained (constraints = h-bonds).
file.mdp.nsteps: nsteps = {value}. How many steps to run. For dynamics the length is nsteps × dt. For minimization it is the most steps mdrun will try before it stops.
file.mdp.emtol: emtol = {value}. Minimization stops when the largest force on any atom drops below this value, in kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> nm<sup>-1</sup>.
file.mdp.emstep: emstep = {value}. The first step size of the minimization, in nm. mdrun grows it when the energy goes down and shrinks it when it goes up.
file.mdp.nstxout: nstxout = {value}. Write the full precision coordinates to the .trr file every this many steps. 0 means never.
file.mdp.nstxout_compressed: nstxout-compressed = {value}. Write a frame to the compressed .xtc trajectory every this many steps. With dt = 0.002 ps, 500 steps is one frame per ps.
file.mdp.nstenergy: nstenergy = {value}. Write the energies to the .edr file every this many steps.
file.mdp.nstlog: nstlog = {value}. Write the energies to the .log file every this many steps.
file.mdp.continuation: continuation = {value}. no means this run starts fresh and the constraints are applied to the starting structure. yes continues from a run that already had them.
file.mdp.constraints: constraints = {value}. h-bonds fixes the length of every bond to a hydrogen. Those bonds vibrate fastest, so fixing them lets us use a 2 fs time step.
file.mdp.constraint_algorithm: constraint_algorithm = {value}. LINCS is the method GROMACS uses to keep the constrained bonds at their length.
file.mdp.cutoff_scheme: cutoff-scheme = {value}. Verlet is the modern neighbor list scheme and the only one that runs on GPUs.
file.mdp.nstlist: nstlist = {value}. How often (in steps) mdrun rebuilds the list of atom pairs close enough to interact. mdrun may raise it on a GPU to run faster.
file.mdp.coulombtype: coulombtype = {value}. How long range electrostatics are handled. PME (particle mesh Ewald) includes every charge in the periodic system, and we use it for anything with water and ions. Cut-off ignores charges beyond rcoulomb.
file.mdp.rcoulomb: rcoulomb = {value}. The cutoff for electrostatics in nm. With PME, charges beyond it are still counted, through the mesh.
file.mdp.rvdw: rvdw = {value}. The cutoff for van der Waals forces in nm. Atoms farther apart than this don't feel each other's van der Waals force.
file.mdp.dispcorr: DispCorr = {value}. Adds back, on average, the van der Waals attraction cut off beyond rvdw. EnerPres corrects both the energy and the pressure, which matters for getting the right density.
file.mdp.pbc: pbc = {value}. Periodic boundary conditions. xyz means the box repeats in every direction, so a molecule leaving one side comes back in on the other.
file.mdp.tcoupl: tcoupl = {value}. The thermostat, which keeps the temperature at ref_t. V-rescale is a good choice for both equilibration and production.
file.mdp.tc_grps: tc-grps = {value}. The groups that get their own thermostat. We couple the protein and everything else (water and ions) separately, so neither heats up the other.
file.mdp.tau_t: tau_t = {value}. How quickly (in ps) each thermostat group is pulled back to its temperature. One number per group in tc-grps.
file.mdp.ref_t: ref_t = {value}. The temperature in K for each group in tc-grps. 300 K is about 27 °C.
file.mdp.pcoupl: pcoupl = {value}. The barostat, which keeps the pressure at ref_p by changing the box size. C-rescale works well for equilibration and production. no keeps the box fixed.
file.mdp.pcoupltype: pcoupltype = {value}. isotropic scales the box the same amount in every direction.
file.mdp.tau_p: tau_p = {value}. How quickly (in ps) the barostat brings the pressure back to ref_p.
file.mdp.ref_p: ref_p = {value}. The pressure in bar. 1 bar is about one atmosphere.
file.mdp.compressibility: compressibility = {value}. How much the system shrinks under pressure, in bar<sup>-1</sup>. 4.5e-5 is the value for water.
file.mdp.refcoord_scaling: refcoord_scaling = {value}. When the box changes size, com moves the restraint positions with the center of mass of the protein. Without it, grompp warns when we use position restraints and pressure coupling together.
file.mdp.gen_vel: gen_vel = {value}. yes gives every atom a random starting velocity for gen_temp. We do this once, at the start of dynamics. Later runs continue with the velocities from the run before.
file.mdp.gen_temp: gen_temp = {value}. The temperature in K used to pick the random starting velocities.
file.mdp.gen_seed: gen_seed = {value}. The seed for the random velocities. The same seed gives the same velocities, and -1 picks a new seed each time.
file.mdp.other: {name} = {value}. We don't have a label for this setting yet. The GROMACS manual lists every .mdp option.
file.mdp.comment: A comment. GROMACS ignores everything after a semicolon.
file.pdb.atom: One atom. In order: the record name, atom number, atom name, residue name, chain, residue number, then x, y and z in Å (not nm), occupancy and B factor.
file.pdb.TITLE: The title, copied from the .gro file.
file.pdb.CRYST1: The box: lengths a, b and c in Å and the angles between them. Our octahedron is stored as a triclinic box, so the angles are not all 90.
file.pdb.MODEL: Starts a model (one frame). A PDB with several frames has a MODEL and an ENDMDL around each one.
